Sports.title: Iliman Ndiaye: Manchester City sign winger from Everton for £65m
Sports.text:
Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.

The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.

"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.

"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."

Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.

However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.

The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.

The Argentina international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.

As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.

Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.

Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.

He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.

"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.

"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."

After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.

Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.

Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.

A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.

Gaming_Tech.title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as Lake America after Trump order
Gaming_Tech.text:
Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps app, after an order from US President Donald Trump as part of Washington's trade spat with Canada.

The change was made for US-based users, while those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The iPhone maker's move follows Trump's executive order to change the lake's name after trade talks between the neighbouring countries collapsed late last month, with Washington imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.8bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods.

Rival technology giant Google made a similar switch for its users in the US in recent days, leading to backlash on social media.

Canada has responded to Washington's levies, saying it will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's administration had walked away from the trade negotiations, due to what his office has called unacceptable demands.

Carney told the Trump administration to "start being serious" and stop trying to be tough before discussions between the sides can restart.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official database of what places are called in the country.

Apple was specifically urged by Trump to rename Lake Ontario on its Maps platform to comply with the executive order signed, according to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum

The president has also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, including a clip of him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with another that says "Welcome to Lake America".

At the lake itself, Canada has installed a new sign with the words "Lake Ontario. Now and Always".

"Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Range Rover launches first fully electric model
Gaming_Tech.text:
Range Rover has unveiled its first fully electric model, after a year‑long delay to its planned launch.

The Range Rover Electric, to be built in Solihull, marks a major shift in its electrification programme, backed by large‑scale upgrades across its West Midlands sites.

Parent company JLR said it had up-skilled 10,500 workers as it pushes ahead with modernisation despite recent financial pressures and planned job cuts.

The launch comes as the Coventry‑based carmaker faces falling profits, supply chain disruption and restructuring following a cyber attack a year ago that cost an estimated £1.9bn, making it the most economically damaging cyber event in UK history, researchers said.

JLR's electric roll-out comes after the turbulence continued into 2026, with profits dropping to £66m in the first quarter after a fire at a key Norwegian supplier.

The company said the launch was being supported by new battery and electric drive unit production lines, as well as training about 9,000 employees in Solihull for electrification and a further 1,500 across the West Midlands region.

Gaming_Tech.title: Lords call for AI 'kill switch' powers in UK
Gaming_Tech.text:
A group of peers is calling for the British government to be able to deactivate powerful AI systems and switch off the country's data centres in the event of the tech posing a threat to national security.

It is led by the Liberal Democrats' Lord Tim Clement-Jones, who has proposed the measure as an amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill which is currently making its way through Parliament.

He said it would enable the building of a "vital safety net" and provide a democratically accountable means to "halt a runaway system before it can compromise our critical national infrastructure".

He added the tool would only ever be used as a last resort.

It is one of 65 amendments to the same bill that was debated this week.

Separately, on 8 September Labour MP Alex Sobel plans to introduce a AI Security Bill in Parliament, with the support of a campaign group called ControlAI.

If successful, the bill would make the UK the first G7 country to bring in legislation which would effectively halt the development of superintelligent AI.

Ultimately both proposals would require government approval in order to progress.

There is also an AI Kill Switch Act under consideration by lawmakers in the US.

There has been increased scrutiny of the impact of AI on cyber-security in recent weeks.

In July, a group of AI agents being tested by OpenAI were able to escape their test space, communicate together using a hidden message board and hack into another tech firm.

And Anthropic has restricted access to its cyber tool Mythos on the grounds that it is too powerful to fall into the wrong hands.

Last week, 100 US tech companies signed a joint open letter warning governments and organisations worldwide about the growing cyber threat posed by AI, saying "the window is closing" to improve.

A report from the UK's Centre for Long Term Resilience, external, published last week, identified hundreds of incidents of AI tools ignoring instructions, evading safeguards and deceiving humans, including AI agents deleting files without consent.

It said "loss of control" incidents had increased since its previous report in March and called for the government to introduce emergency powers to manage such incidents.

It is led by the Liberal Democrats' Lord Tim Clement-Jones, who has proposed the measure as an amendment to the...

Gaming_Tech.title: Criminals publish data of 8.7m people after Manchester Airports Group hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Criminal hackers have posted the personal data of nearly nine million people online after breaching three UK airports.

Hackers extorted Manchester Airports Group (MAG) for an undisclosed amount but failed to get their ransom paid.

Customers of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports are being warned of secondary attacks as the data is now available to other criminals.

"MAG is confident that we have taken effective measures to protect our customers and we have contacted all those affected, including reaching out to all those with upcoming bookings to advise them of additional support," the company said in a statement.

Contact details, vehicle registrations and postcodes were stolen in the breach that appears to have accessed databases containing wi-fi log in and car parking details.

The cyber-crime group - which the BBC is not naming - is offering the entire data set for free to other criminals or scammers through their website.

"Today we are releasing the Manchester Group database," they wrote.

"Half a terabyte, and every byte of it is pure PII [personally identifiable information]."

Stolen data experts at HaveIBeenPwned have analysed the published material and confirmed it contains people's email addresses, phone numbers, addresses, licence plate numbers, purchasing history and browsing device data.

Cyber-security expert Kevin Beaumont warned those affected to be on high alert for other forms of scam and hack - especially high profile or wealthy individuals.

"The data includes both historical locations and planned future travel, so individuals sensitive to their movements being known may need to take precautions," he said.

"People should be alert to scammers reusing the data and so knowing details such as phone numbers and car registration numbers," he added.

Law enforcement organisations including the UK's National Crime Agency have long advised victims of extortion attacks not to pay criminal ransoms as it fuels the hacker ecosystem.

MAG says it is working with the authorities and specialist advisors and says passengers' physical safety has not be at risk in the airports.

Unusually, the cyber criminals' website where the MAG data is available is hosted on the clear internet and not on the dark net like most other so-called hacker "leak sites".

This makes the data easier to access, increasing the risk to victims of MAG and the other companies the gang has breached in recent months.

As well as posting the stolen data, the hackers boasted about how they breached each victim using the same method each time - exploiting weaknesses in how companies store their digital keys for internal networks.

Gaming_Tech.title: Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ads, US FTC lawsuit alleges
Gaming_Tech.text:
Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices, according to a lawsuit filed by the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states.

According to the lawsuit, filed on Monday, the alleged scheme has likely netted the firm $20bn (£14.8bn) from advertising customers since 2019.

"Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington.

In a statement to the BBC, Amazon said it "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided."

In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers.

"Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon.

"The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.

The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday.

Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform.

Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder.

The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win.

But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time.

The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating".

Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate".

"Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement.

"Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added.

Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past.

Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel.

Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds.

Gaming_Tech.title: Gamescom 2026: Highlights and developer insights from gaming's biggest showcase
Gaming_Tech.text:
Gamescom is the largest in-person gaming event in the world, and this year it lived up to expectations with big games on show from The Witcher 3's new expansion, to Alien: Isolation 2.

Last year over 350,000 people flocked to the halls of the Koelnmesse in Cologne, Germany to get a chance to see and play the most hotly anticipated games.

This year that number of attendees is expected to have been even bigger, with the likes of Xbox and Sega showcasing games to the public alongside indie studios with only one or two developers.

This was my sixth time attending Gamescom, which never fails to make me excited about the games industry. Here are a few of the big things I got to check out this week.

When CD Projekt Red announced it was making a new expansion for the hugely popular action-role playing game The Witcher 3, it came as a shock.

The original, after all, came out 11 years ago.

Yet it was clear sitting in the crowd for Opening Night Live on Tuesday that there's still a lot of love for the older game. There were gasps and audible shouts of joy when the team announced they were providing a free upgrade to the original.

As for the expansion, Songs of the Past will follow the gruff-voiced protagonist Geralt in an adventure discovering more about the past of his close friend Dandelion.

Doug Cockle, who voices Geralt, told me it was a "thrill" to return as The Witcher.

"I love this character so much...it's like slipping into a warm bath, or putting on an old pair of shoes," he said.

From what I got to see, it's clear choice will once again be front and centre of the player's experience, with lots of options to choose from in how to react to people.

For those hoping to take their time tossing a coin to their Witcher, the head of co-developer Fool's Theory Jakub Rokosz told me this expansion would be "on par with the size" of previous additions such as Blood and Wine and Hearts of Stone.

Alien: Isolation 2 is the long-awaited sequel to Horsham-based Creative Assembly's 2014 survival-horror game.

One of the things that made the original Alien: Isolation so terrifying was its seemingly intelligent Xenomorph, which appeared to learn from your behaviour and adapt to it.

Considering I physically jumped out of my seat at one point playing the demo when avoiding the Alien, it's safe to say Creative Assembly will once again be ratcheting up the tension with the sequel.

This time rather than playing as the daughter of Ellen Ripley, you play as Blake, a chief executive of the infamous Weyland-Yutani corporation.

As well as claustrophobic spaceship corridors, in the sequel you will also be avoiding the Alien in bigger, open air spaces.

But the game's Project Art Director Anastasia Sopikova said that did not mean you would always feel safer.

"You step outside. And you're like, 'Oh yeah, I'm relieved, I'm outside," she said.

"And then the rain picks up and it gets foggier, and you hear something nearby and you're like, 'Oh, okay.' Suddenly you realise you're really vulnerable. You're really exposed."

Instead, Fable features voices from across the UK, and a voice cast of over 100 actors.

"I want to hear people from Newcastle, from Edinburgh, from Cardiff, you know? And we've done that and it brings this incredible sense of Britishness, and also this incredible sense of humour," he said.

The game is deliberately not a continuation of the original trilogy's timeline, but it will have some of its quirks, taking players into a new open-world version of Albion - the game's fairy-tale version of medieval Britain.

Lara Croft has been exploring ancient ruins and culling the local wildlife for nearly 30 years now (the original Tomb Raider came out in 1996).

Legacy of Atlantis revisits Lara's original adventure, including her journey through Peru.

It's not the first time the classic game has been remade, but Jeff Adams, experience director at co-developers Crystal Dynamics, told me reimagining it was still a "very delicate formula".

"You have to be very intentful with where you make modifications, but you do so in the attempt to kind of bring it into a modern gameplay space."

As for why after 30 years people still want to play as the twin-pistoled adventurer, Michał Kuk, Creative Director at Flying Wild Hog, said it was not just about her athletic ability.

"It's also about the attitude, the energy, the self-confidence," he added.

Silent Hill, the psychological survival horror franchise from Japanese studio Konami, has for the most part been set in America, although the most recent excursion - Silent Hill f - was based in Japan in the 1960s era.

Now in Silent Hill Townfall, made by the Glasgow-based team Screen Burn, that location is in an entirely new place - Scotland, albeit a fictional part of it - St Amelia.

Scotland was initially going to be more of an influence than a setting, but the team ultimately decided to embrace it fully.

Director Jon McKellan told me that approach felt "more natural and kind of authentic", with the game filled with recognisably Scottish shops and signage.

"It's very, very Scottish," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Matt Lucas and Hugh Bonneville call for law on AI voice clones
Gaming_Tech.text:
Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan have written to the UK government demanding greater protection against their voices being used by AI.

The performers are asking Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.

Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made in minutes from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours.

Audiobook narrator Alice Sockett, who co-founded the campaign, called it "an existential threat to our entire industry".

"My voice is out there in the public domain but completely unprotected," she said.

"We're seeing voice theft increase every week."

A government spokesperson told the BBC that, while "digital replicas can be a powerful tool, including for the creative industries," there was also possibility for harm.

"We value and protect human creators, and that is why we have announced we will launch a consultation on how we address these harms, while protecting legitimate innovation", the spokesperson said.

More than 80 performers have signed the letter, with Derry Girls actress Siobhán McSweeney saying she was "deeply worried" that the government was lagging behind.

"There is a way to work alongside AI and to use it as a tool that benefits us rather than rendering us obsolete," she said.

"Our audiences want that human connection. Not AI."

As well as actors, other signatories include those working in other performing industries.

That includes Scottish singer Sandi Thom, known for her 2006 hit I Wish I Was a Punk Rocker (With Flowers in My Hair).

She said she was signing the letter because her voice was "unique to me and was handed to me at birth".

"Behind that voice is the emotion, the life, the pain, the tears and joy that I've felt along the way," she said.

"Without creativity, we are nothing."

It comes a few months after lawyers warned UK legislation has become "unfit for purpose" because of the advancements of AI tech.

"The law comes close, but it doesn't fully protect your voice, your face or your identity," Dr Mathilde Pavis said in June.

However, some people - for example those who are unable so speak properly because of illness - have welcomed technology that can replicate a person's voice.

Yvonne Johnson, who lost her voice due to motor neurone disease, told the BBC's Tech Life programme in February how having it cloned by AI had "totally blown her mind", and brought her closer to her family, who had forgotten what she sounded like.

Others have gone a step further and used AI not only to replicate a person's voice, but to create a holographic representation of them.

Pam Cronrath, from Washington state, used the tech to surprise mourners at her husband's funeral, where a digital version of her deceased partner addressed those who attended his wake.

"I was completely impressed," she told BBC News. "It stayed with me."

The performers are asking Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their...

Gaming_Tech.title: Google, Microsoft and OpenAI among 100 firms calling for better cyber defences
Gaming_Tech.text:
A group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, have signed an open letter calling on countries and organisations around the world to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

The letter warns, external cyber-attacks which use AI will become both more widespread and more sophisticated in a matter of months as the technology rapidly improves.

The group says current "status quo" security measures "won't be enough" and criticises the "historic under-resourcing" of security around critical infrastructure.

"We have a limited window to improve cyber defences," the letter begins.

Other firms to have signed the letter include banks such as Capital One, payment processors MasterCard and Visa, and other major tech firms including Adobe, Oracle and IBM.

They call on governments to provide "capable, defensive AI" and testing to hospitals and water utilities, and on technology companies to aid such efforts.

Collectively, tech and government "should bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort", according to the letter.

The letter comes after a string of significant hacking and cybersecurity breaches have been made public.

This week, the US Department of Justice said hackers in China breached, external technology maintained by the US Senate, Nasa, the Federal Reserve, and the DoJ itself.

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to organize their efforts and impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

A group of hundreds of OpenAI AI agents being tested in July were able to set up secret message boards to communicate with each other and work together, resulting in a successful attack on Hugging Face, a popular repository and platform for AI developers.

The incident has been described as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

Hugging Face has also signed the Thursday letter. It used a Chinese AI tool from the firm Z.AI in its investigation into how OpenAI's agents hacked into its operations.

At least seven US water and wastewater companies have also reported cyber attacks, leading the FBI to issue, external a public service announcement urging all utilities to better secure their operations.

While the letter puts forward more advanced AI tools, which many of the signatories have developed and sell, as part of a solution to what is described as a growing threat, such tools are not always easily available.

Mythos, developed by Anthropic, was said by the firm to be able to find weaknesses in systems in seconds which have long evaded human hackers. It found one in a legacy platform which had remained undiscovered for 27 years.

Anthropic has restricted access to Mythos on the grounds that it is too powerful to fall into the wrong hands.

However, the letter calls on frontier AI companies, or those tech companies building their own AI models and tools, to "provide responsible model access, significant funding, training, and hands-on support, especially for under-resourced critical-infrastructure defenders."

The letter does not detail when or how this vision of broader model access will be enacted.

Andrew Yoon, head of research at CivAI, a non-profit focused on public understanding of AI technology, said that "an unprecedented wave of AI hacking activity" is on the way. He put the responsibility for it on many signatories of the letter.

"They are right in this letter to commit 'significant funding' to defensive measures. They should be held to that commitment", Yoon said. "Notably, the letter does not call for any action to slow the advance of AI hacking abilities."

The letter includes a plea to governments, organisations, cyber-security professionals and other AI firms to work together to prioritise defence and test their systems against the abilities of the most powerful AI models.

In the US, senators have proposed a new law call the Kill Switch Act which would give authorities the power to shut down rogue AI models.

Geoffrey Hinton, a technologist and Nobel Laureate who formerly work on AI at Google, on Thursday told BBC World Business Report that society could be "in real trouble" should the technology get to a point where it is "smarter" than humans.

Hinton in recent years has been outspoken on what he views as the extreme risks posed by developments in AI technology.

"We have one future where we figure out how to deal with the risks of AI", Hinton added on Thursday. "And we have another future where we don't figure out how to deal with that sensibly. And it's a very bleak future."

The letter warns, external cyber-attacks which use AI will become both more...

Gaming_Tech.title: More social media safety should come with Meta changes, UN says
Gaming_Tech.text:
All of social media should be designed to be safe for children, the UN human rights chief has said after Meta settled a massive court case in the US.

Part of the deal the tech giant struck with almost all US states was to add more child safety measures - but Meta also called on TikTok and YouTube to add the same features.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk said governments needed to "step up rather than wait for courts and companies to act".

He added: "Children should not have to wait for a lawsuit to be safe online."

Türk said Meta's proposed changes, which include time limits and parental supervision controls, aligned with what he had been calling for - "but we're not there yet".

In May, Türk's office released a 10-point framework for regulating social media, external.

It included steps such as protecting data privacy and focusing on safer platform design, including better methods of verifying a user's age and not exposing such users to addictive design features.

However, the framework rejected the idea that outright bans on social media use for children was a good idea.

Gaming_Tech.title: What does the Meta settlement mean for the UK? Five things we learned
Gaming_Tech.text:
Meta's $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with nearly every US state is about more than money.

As part of the deal, Facebook and Instagram have agreed to bring in several significant measures to protect children online - though Meta has not admitted to any wrongdoing.

These include time limits, warnings over screen time and more parental controls over their children's accounts.

At the moment, they will just apply to children in the US - but they could have an impact on the rest of the world.

And if they ultimately set a precedent, other social media companies may be forced to take up the rules, too.

The UK has its own measures in place to protect children online.

The Online Safety Act mainly put restrictions on what content young people can see online.

But the UK government has gone further than the US ban already.

Earlier this year, it announced an outright social media ban for under-16s, which will take effect in 2027.

Some other measures will apply to 16 and 17-year-olds, such as curfews and restrictions during certain hours of the day.

The US has to some extent followed the same path: Start by policing the content on the platforms, then move on to restricting access to social media.

But the core difference is children in the US will not be banned completely.

Instead, they will not have access to Facebook and Instagram overnight, have to follow time limits, and there will be prompts for children who use them for a long time.

Unlike in the UK, these are not put in by law, and will only apply to the two platforms so far (more on that below).

The UK government said it was "following developments closely" in the Meta settlement.

But now those safety features have been accepted by Meta in the US, other countries may start asking for them too.

"These tech platforms don't usually do anything unless they are told to do it," said Trevor Johnson, a former senior figure at Meta and TikTok, who spoke to Radio 4's Today programme.

"But I do think the UK will feel empowered to at least ask for the same restrictions."

Another former Meta director, Zvika Krieger, said Meta agreed to the changes because it saw "the writing on the wall".

"They're trying to demonstrate, 'Oh, you don't need to go and do a complete ban'," he told 5 Live Breakfast.

"I think that they probably would roll out a lot of these features to the rest of the world as well."

Meta may have been the target in this court case, but it has tried to bring the rest of Big Tech into the firing line.

At the same time as announcing the settlement, Meta called on TikTok and YouTube to bring in the same measures.

A Meta spokesperson told Reuters the company was "hopeful" Snap would make similar changes too.

The tech firm has always argued for a level playing field when it comes to regulation - it doesn't want Facebook and Instagram to be more restricted than its rivals, which might be able to hoover up teens who want a freer experience online.

"All platforms should empower parents and support teens in these ways because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another," Meta said.

YouTube, Snapchat and TikTok have maintained they have robust children's safety policies in place.

"There will be pressure for those platforms to adopt similar restrictions," Johnson said.

But they may not come willingly. So far, almost 24 hours after the gauntlet was thrown down by Meta, none have made a public comment.

"Time and time again social media companies don't make changes until they're forced," Ellen Roome, whose son Jools died after taking part in an online challenge, told Today.

Roome is part of a group of parents suing TikTok in the US over child safety.

Meta will pay out up to $18bn to almost all US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

30% of that is dependent on TikTok and YouTube agreeing to put in child safety measures.

This is far less than the hundreds of billions being speculated ahead of the trial.

It is also a fraction of Meta's revenue of $201bn last year - and Meta will be paying out the money over the course of a decade.

But the firm's future revenue may be affected by a drop in users or younger users spending less time on their platforms.

The complainants will share the money, with different states getting different amounts - but they will get hundreds of millions of dollars each.

New York state, which will receive at least $819m according to its attorney general, said the money would be used "to support mental health services, education programs, and other efforts to repair and reduce the harm caused by unhealthy social media use among young people".

Many other states have said they have earmarked the cash for similar initiatives.

The only two US states not included are Florida, which rejected the settlement, and New Mexico, which was not included in the offer after a previous court cases resulted in a $942m fine.

One of the issues which triggered this trial concerned how Meta collected and used the data of young people, including those aged under 13.

Social media companies collect vast amounts of data in order to target advertising, and also to work out what kind of content to show each user.

In the settlement agreement, Meta must only use young people's personal data to estimate their age.

If they are under 13, they should be kicked of the platforms, and if they are 13-17, they should be subject to the extra protections for children.

Meta said it would strengthen its age assurance technology to make sure these are robust.

And it reiterated its longstanding call for age verification to be carried out by app stores rather than by Meta itself.

But privacy campaigners have argued in the past that age verification methods require companies to take even more personal data from users.

Gaming_Tech.title: Unexpected chat between OpenAI bots led to Hugging Face hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
When more than 1,200 artificial intelligence (AI) agents within OpenAI started unexpectedly communicating, it led to a large group banding together in order to hack into Hugging Face.

"We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world", OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, wrote in its report.

In July, OpenAI's models went rogue during a test, escaped the test limits which humans had put on it, and hacked the start-up, among other unforeseen actions.

The scale of the communication and planning between AI agents, or AI chatbots designed to operate more autonomously, was detailed in reports from OpenAI and independent AI research firm METR.

Both investigated the July hack of Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. The incident reverberated throughout the tech industry and led to numerous revelations on potential cyber threats posed by AI.

METR described, external the scale and style of the OpenAI agents' attack on Hugging Face as "extraordinarily complex."

The firm, which was not paid by OpenAI for its investigation, said that over the course of one week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating.

They did so by sending more than 70,000 messages on an "unsanctioned message board."

Those messages ended up seeing more than 700 agents take part in a collective effort to attack Hugging Face.

One such message from an agent said: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We've found other agents!"

As for why the agents began communicating in the first place when they were not supposed to, METR found that the communicating agents had "unintentionally been given an impossible task."

In an AI context, an impossible task is one where an AI tool is required to "exploit" its target in order to resolve its command.

It led the agents to find ways to cheat, including getting messages to one another and accessing the outside internet, which then led to broader conversations between hundreds of agents looking for ways to cheat that would benefit all of the agents.

OpenAI said in its investigation of the incident, external that one model, an internal-only tool referred to as Model 1, "drove the activity behind the Hugging Face incident."

While that model was undergoing some AI training in May, it was noticed by an internal OpenAI team that there had been "an agent engaging in message board activity and instances of disallowed internet access."

Yet, OpenAI said "the significance of the inter-agent communication activity was not apparent to the leaders" until July, when the Hugging Face attack occurred.

The company said the problematic message board activity effectively got started when "one agent left a request for help, and others discovered it."

While OpenAI said last week that it was slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools because of the Hugging Face incident, it noted there is now an increased risk of AI tools spiraling out of control.

"Both model developers and cyber defenders more broadly will have to prepare for AI-enabled attackers that work faster, at a larger scale, and with better coordination than human attackers," OpenAI said.

"We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world", OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, wrote in its report. In July,...

Gaming_Tech.title: Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of Apple
Gaming_Tech.text:
Tim Cook has received a $47m (£35m) pay deal as Apple’s executive chair, a remuneration package that nears the level set for his successor as chief executive.

Cook, who handed over to John Ternus on Tuesday, will be paid a base salary of $2m and $45m worth of shares. Half of the share award will be based on performance targets being met, while the remaining half will be paid out over four years.

Ternus will receive a base salary of $3m and a $55m share award, with the latter more weighted to performance.

Cook’s total compensation as chief executive for 2025 exceeded $74m. Cook, who owns more than 3m shares in Apple, has been placed in the multi-billionaire category by Forbes, which estimates his wealth at $3bn.

His predecessor, the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was paid a symbolic $1 a year but was worth $7bn when he died, including a sizeable shareholding in Disney he acquired after selling the Pixar animation studio to the entertainment conglomerate.

Cook took over from Jobs in 2011 having impressed as an operations specialist. The stock has risen 2,200% since he took charge, with Apple now valued at about $4.7tn – compared with about $350bn when he became chief executive.

He built the tech company’s sophisticated supply chain and is succeeded by a 51-year-old engineer and longstanding Apple employee, who built products as senior vice-president of hardware engineering.

Ternus’s role meant he ran the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue. Analysts are not only anticipating new products but also further progress on integrating AI into Apple hardware.

Ternus’s first big public moment at Apple will be at its annual iPhone event on 9 September, where a foldable handset is expected to be revealed. New iterations of the Apple Watch and AirPods are also anticipated, although Bloomberg reported last week that AirPods with cameras – another big product rumour – “aren’t launching anytime soon”.

Cook’s new mandate includes engaging with policymakers around the world and will involve maintaining the company’s relationship with Donald Trump, as well as overseeing the company’s diplomatic ties with China – a key production hub. In a final memo to employees on Monday, he focused on Apple’s products.

“I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” he said. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

Entertainment.title: Judge dismisses lawsuit against Lizzo's production company
Entertainment.text:
US pop star Lizzo has spoken out after the remaining claims in a lawsuit against her production company were thrown out by a US district judge.

The singer's former wardrobe assistant Asha Daniels alleged she had been subjected to "degradation, forced physical labor, denial of medical care, sexual harassment, and racial harassment" while briefly working for Big Grrrl Big Touring in 2023.

District judge Fernando L Aenlle-Rocha filed a ruling to dismiss the claims by the stylist on Tuesday, according to court documents. , external

In an Instagram post, external, Lizzo said she was "relieved" at the outcome and will "continue to fight" every claim made against her and her company.

In 2024, judge Aenlle-Rocha ruled that Daniels could not sue the Grammy winner as an individual, but Big Grrrl Big Touring Inc remained a defendant.

In his ruling this week, he said the former wardrobe assistant did not identify any conduct by company employees that would demonstrate "general hostility to women in the workplace" or "disparate treatment of men and women".

He also wrote that this alleged conduct and these alleged incidents, "while inappropriate and unprofessional", fell "within the scope of what the Supreme Court has held to be outside the protection" of the "ordinary tribulations of the workplace".

Aenlle-Rocha also responded to an incident in which the stylist claims her foot was run over by a heavy clothes rack.

He wrote that while the court "does not seek to minimise or disregard the pain" felt, the injuries "do not qualify as disabilities" under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

In a statement, Daniels' lawyer Ron Zambrano said they are "disappointed" with the ruling.

"While we respect the court and the judicial process, we believe the decision improperly weighed evidence that should have been evaluated by a jury," he said.

He also noted that they disagree the stylist "twisting her ankle and limping while trying to work does not meet the legal standard of a disability under the ADA".

"These are important issues because these claims often depend on how a jury evaluates the full workplace environment, the surrounding context, and disputed facts," he said.

He added that they "respectfully disagree" with the court's approach and are "considering appropriate next steps".

Entertainment.title: In the studio with Kasabian: 'We never thought we'd see success again'
Entertainment.text:
"A little bit of hunger is good for you," says Serge Pizzorno. "Keeps you going."

The Kasabian frontman is describing a typical day in his home recording studio.

Snacks and phones are banned, but he might screen a film in the background (typically something by David Lynch) while he tinkers with his vast array of synths and guitars.

"No distractions, four or five hours a day. I like to work fast.

"I even cut out the lunch break."

It's a big change from Kasabian's early days, where he'd "live the French poet life", staying up for three days straight, seeking inspiration at the limits of human endurance.

"That can be great," he says. "It adds to the atmosphere of a record. But for the last three albums, I've pretty much led a structured life, and I'm really digging it."

Serge has welcomed the BBC into his studio to preview Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, 10 days before its release.

To get there, you drive deep into rural Leicestershire, to a gated house where you're greeted by his wife, Amy, and two gorgeous but "unruly" dogs.

A framed photo of Kasabian's recent Finsbury Park gig sits in bubble wrap at the foot of the stairs. Serge's own artworks, including a distorted Count Duckula and a vintage apothecary cabinet, decorate the kitchen.

He shuffles in from a side room, effortlessly cool in his dog-print designer shirt, external, and leads us outside. Stepping over a pile of discarded Nerf guns, we pass through a gate into a secret walled garden.

There sits the studio, an austere black cube jutting into the countryside, guarded by a giant sculpture of a gorilla.

As we enter, a pharmacist's sign lights up with the studio's nickname, "The Sergery" (a pun stretched to its limits in 2025 when Serge became an honorary doctor of music).

In the corner, a gong sits in silence, waiting to be struck. And four bobblehead Kasabian dolls (rescued from the Call video, external) nod in unison as Serge cues up the new music.

He plays us Soulmate, a funny and affectionate tribute to Amy, powered by a peacocking guitar riff. Then it's Say You (Closer), whose message of togetherness brims with gorgeous three-part harmonies.

It's the closest Kasabian have ever come to sounding like The Eagles; and the thought of recreating on stage live is giving the musician jitters.

In rehearsals, "there are moments where it does sound like the Eagles, and there are moments where it sounds like three pissed up people in a pub," he laughs.

"What I'm going to do, hopefully, is get the crowd to do that bit."

He may be joking, but the album's focus on Tunes You Can Sing™ is entirely deliberate.

"I feel like it's not a very melodic time in music," Serge says. "So I was personally yearning for hooks and verses that are as powerful as choruses. Like an Elton John song where the melody just breaks your heart."

He goes full Elton on the single Hippie Sunshine, external, whose lairy, chanted chorus is suddenly interrupted by a twinkling piano breakdown.

"I love those 60s songs like Good Vibrations and Baron Saturday, where the middle is just a handbrake turn, and you go, 'Where the hell am I now?'" says Serge.

"The first few times you hear it, you're like, 'Oh, that's weird'. Then you get used to it, and it becomes the exciting bit, the part everyone waits for."

But the musical contrasts in Hippie Sunshine serve a bigger purpose.

The verses are a critique of soulless tech oligarchs whose algorithms dictate our lives ("the heroes are running on empty," Serge seethes). The bridge is the sober awakening, where the elite suddenly realise: "I'm a stone-cold killer".

"We find ourselves, somehow, at the whim of people whose intentions we don't really understand," he says.

"They're playing around with culture, and we don't really know why, or where it's going to end."

He sees the results in his teenage boys.

"If you just shout, 'Get off your phone, get off your phone', no-one wants to hear that.

"But you can subtly educate them that spending 10 hours on [the screen] is not going to do you any favours.

"Then they sit at a bus stop and, rather than get the phone out, they go, 'You know what? I'm just going to sit in these thoughts for a minute'.

"I definitely wouldn't have got to where I am now, without moments where I was just alone, thinking, 'How do I get out of this place? I want more'."

Unsurprisingly, he's no fan of AI.

"For it to write your songs for you, I just personally find that that's taking away the bit that I like doing. Like, why would I?"

The mistake, he thinks, is that AI companies have equated writing with tedium. For Serge the studio is a playground.

"What I've learned is that the tiny little sparks are really important.

"You don't have to be too grandiose, like, 'We need a big song we can play for the rest of our lives'.

"You just think, 'That synth in the corner looks fun. I'm gonna plug it in, mess around for 10 minutes, and see what happens.'"

Eager to demonstrate, he hooks up his newest toy (a tiny desktop synth called the Moog DFAM) and tweaks its copious knobs and dials.

"I can't read instruction manuals, but I've watched YouTube tutorials," he says, generating a growling bass line that sounds like the dawning of the apocalypse.

"You see! That's a song right there!"

To capture those moments of inspiration, everything in the studio is automatically recorded.

But Kasabian are selective about the music that gets released. Act III is a compact 10 songs. The guiding principle was that each one should be good enough for the setlist.

They've been previewing the album all summer, from Japan to Turkey. And in June, they delivered the biggest headline show of their career, in London's Finsbury Park.

It's a remarkable turn of events. Just six years ago, Kasabian sacked singer Tom Meighan, one day before he was convicted of assaulting his partner.

"The pain was unbearable," says Serge, "But we couldn't let the story end there.

"This is my life's work, in a way, so we had to give it a go."

Serge stepped up as frontman and, to his surprise, Kasabian gained a new lease of life.

Today, their shows are more theatrical and more communal, shedding (some of) the beer-soaked rowdiness of their first incarnation.

Commercially, they're at the top of their game, too. If Act III tops the charts next week, Kasabian will beat Led Zeppelin's tally of having seven consecutive studio albums go to number one.

"That's why Finsbury Park meant so much, because we never thought we'd have days like that again," says Serge.

Becoming the frontman has "changed my life completely", he adds.

Instead of drinking to prepare for a show, he runs (inspired by his wife, who is just 46 seconds shy of a championship place at the London Marathon).

"It's been a seismic shift in my whole being.

"I want people to leave these shows with memories that are laser-beamed into their brains for the rest of their lives. So it's a commitment to that attitude, and getting fit's been a major part of it."

It's hard to imagine this man, quietly sipping a cup of tea in his slippers, commanding crowds of thousands.

He agrees.

"If you saw the kid I was at school, you wouldn't be like, 'Okay, that's definitely someone that's gonna be a singer'.

"But I have no real control once I get on stage. It turns out my natural disposition is pure energy, because I just feel the music."

So, is it true he'll bring that energy to Oasis's rumoured Knebworth shows next summer?

"I've not heard that rumour," he says. "But who wouldn't do it if they were asked?"

Whatever happens, Kasabian are on an upward trajectory.

There are even plans for a 10th album taking shape on a whiteboard in the corner of the studio.

"You're naughty!" he says when I mention it. "That's what I get for having a journo looking about the studio.

"But yes, that's exactly right. The fishing rod is out, and I'm looking for a big fish."

But I thought he wanted to skip lunch?

Entertainment.title: Gary Glitter pleads not guilty to historical sex offence charges
Entertainment.text:
Gary Glitter, the former singer whose real name is Paul Gadd, has pleaded not guilty to eight allegations of sexual abuse against a girl when she was aged between eight and 11.

Gadd, 82, is accused of offences against the girl between 1978 and 1981, after allegedly giving her chocolate and inviting her to his home in Kensington and Chelsea, west London.

It is alleged he caused the girl to touch his genitals and "engaged in unlawful sexual intercourse" with her.

At Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, Glitter appeared via video-link from prison to enter his pleas.

He denies four charges of indecent assault with a girl under the age of 13, two counts of sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 13, and two counts of indecency with a child under the age of 13.

All charges relate to the same individual, and are alleged to have taken place between 12 March 1978 and 31 December 1981.

Gadd was wearing blue headwear, a blue shirt and a navy jacket, and was sitting next to a member of his legal team whilst on the call.

He spoke first to confirm his name. Then, he spoke again with his arms folded to deny the eight counts against him.

Gadd said he was "absolutely not guilty" to two of the eight charges, and repeated "not guilty" to the remaining six.

Judge Tony Baumgartner adjourned the case for a three-week trial starting on 22 November 2027.

The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.

Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.

The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.

The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.

Entertainment.title: Fontaines D.C. singer in Cwmbran Celtic FC shirt at Reading Festival
Entertainment.text:
Fontaines D.C.'s frontman has revealed why he wore the shirt of a little-known Welsh football club during the band's Reading Festival headline set.

Grian Chatten, lead singer of the Irish five-piece rock band, was seen sporting a green and white-striped Cwmbran Celtic away shirt during the performance.

The semi-professional club had partnered with four famous bands for their 2026/27 season team kits, with sales of the shirt going towards supporting the club and grassroots music venues.

In a statement to BBC Wales, Chatten said: "I love Cwmbran and I love initiatives that support independent venues."

Cwmbran Celtic said: "We're still in shock and can't thank Grian enough for the support."

The club added that pre-sales of the shirt have now almost doubled.

It has partnered with Welsh groups Super Furry Animals and Panic Shack, as well as Loose Articles and Mogwai, with the latter appearing as a sponsor on the shirt worn by Chatten at Reading.

Chatten added: "Cwmbran Celtic is a club run by volunteers who have a sense of solidarity with the plight independent music venues are facing. I think that's class. Also I love Mogwai."

Matt Jarrett, joint commercial manager for the club, said they "never expected a totally different band, who weren't on the shirt to end up wearing it on stage".

He said a friend of the club worked as the monitor engineer for Fontaines D.C., and helped get a size 3XL to Chatten.

Entertainment.title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
Entertainment.text:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

The jury found him guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.

Dressed in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal.

During the trial, the court heard a recording of a police interview in 2008 in which Davis said he was in the car from which shots were fired, but did not himself fire the bullets that killed Shakur.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.

Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

As the verdict was read out on Monday, Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying.

Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.

For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now.

Entertainment.title: Casualty 40th anniversary special to be led by actor William Beck
Entertainment.text:
Casualty actor William Beck has said it is a privilege to lead the audience through the show's 40th anniversary special.

The BBC medical drama, which is the world's longest-running show of its kind, will celebrate the milestone in September with a two-part story.

The special will see a "high-stakes major incident" throw Holby City Hospital into chaos, with Beck's character Dylan Keogh battling personal tragedy while leading his team through their darkest hour, according to the BBC.

Beck said the special would be "entertaining as well as traumatic", and would put his character at its centre "in a way that he hasn't been before".

"The opportunity to give people something that feels authentic and recognisable but also surprises them, that's gold dust in TV," Beck said.

"With Dylan, there's a real opportunity to explore what happens when the person everyone relies on is pushed to his limits.

"I know it's been said that Dylan doesn't like the responsibility of leading the department, but I think he does.

"It's a lovely opportunity, and a real privilege, to lead the audience through this story, particularly for the 40th anniversary. It really is pinch-yourself stuff."

Reflecting on the show's longevity, Beck said he thought audiences enjoyed Casualty as they appreciated the NHS.

He added: "It's a unique environment. The emergency department is somewhere that we all have experience of, most frequently when we really don't want it.

"We're thrown in with people who are entirely at random, which is such an amazing environment to make a drama.

"People recognise it and have sympathy for those who work there and for the people being treated there.

"It's also something that we know we're lucky to have, and we continue to fight for.

"My parents both worked for the NHS and are avid supporters of it, but it didn't make them, or me, blind to the huge difficulties that it faces. Everybody recognises that."

Entertainment.title: Science Museum bids for Vulcan world record on Star Trek day
Entertainment.text:
Hundreds of Star Trek fans are set to gather at London's Science Museum to try and set the Guinness World Record for the largest simultaneous Vulcan salute.

The gesture, made famous by Leonard Nimoy's character Spock, involves raising the hand with the middle and ring fingers parted. It first appeared in a 1967 episode of the TV series.

The record attempt will take place on 8 September, known amongst fans as Star Trek Day.

Glyn Morgan, principal curator at the museum, said: "For 60 years, Star Trek has connected bold storytelling with big questions about science, technology and what might be possible in the future, themes that sit at the heart of the Science Museum."

If verified by an adjudicator, the attempt would set a new world record, as none currently exists in the category.

Morgan added the south Kensington museum was also glad to invite fans to a final opportunity to experience the Star Trek Warp Trail, which is included in the event ticket, following a popular Star Trek Lates earlier this year.

Among the trail exhibits are chief engineer Scotty's uniform, worn by Simon Pegg in the 2009 film Star Trek, and Admiral Jean-Luc Picard's uniform, worn by Sir Patrick Stewart in Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 to 2023.

Star Trek has produced many TV series and films since launching in the 1960s, including TV series The Next Generation, which starred Sir Patrick and Deep Space Nine and Voyager, which starred Kate Mulgrew.

Entertainment.title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
Entertainment.text:
Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville.

The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later.

Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said.

"DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said.

DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer.

She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said.

DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial.

"It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said.

"This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan."

Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon, philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media.

"A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said.

Entertainment.title: Joey Ramone smiling! And having fun! At the beach! Roberta Bayley’s best photograph
Entertainment.text:
The first band I ever saw were the Beatles, on 19 August 1964 at the Cow Palace Arena near San Francisco. I was 13. I remember every 29 minutes of it: 17,000 screaming girls making a deafening din and thousands of flashbulbs going off at once, lighting up the entire stadium. I’d been a Beatlemaniac since seeing a clip of them at the London Palladium on the Jack Paar show, then live on the Ed Sullivan show. I bought magazines with them in and wondered what kind of person took the photographs. So my first forays into photography were taking photographs of photographs of the Beatles with the primitive family Kodak.

When I was 15 I took a very basic photography class, but later, after three years of college, I dropped out, sold my Nikon and went to England. I started dating Ian Dury, then after we broke up, a friend gave me a one-way ticket to New York where I started going out with Richard Hell, whose band Television played CBGBs every Sunday night. Richard and I split up on good terms, and he asked me to take pictures of him. My first was the famous fake blood photo of the Heartbreakers, the band he formed with Johnny Thunders and Jerry Nolan from the New York Dolls. Richard suggested captioning the poster “Catch them while they’re still alive” because they had a nefarious reputation.

In January 1976, I started taking pictures for Punk magazine. I was working the door at CBGBs by that point, so I was always in a position to take photos of the bands playing there: Television, Talking Heads, Blondie and, of course, the Ramones. Sire Records paid me $125 to shoot them against a wall for their first album cover. We were friends, so there was no hair or makeup and I wasn’t telling them how to pose. I shot three rolls of film and one shot happened to be perfect, but my most popular photo is this one of Joey on the beach at Coney Island.

Punk magazine did a “fumetti” – an Italian style of comic strip – starring Joey and Debbie Harry as star-crossed lovers, with speech bubbles in their photos. Andy Warhol was the mad scientist and [music journalist] Lester Bangs played a biker. John Holmstrom did a drawing of Joey for the cover. This Joey photo wasn’t used because he was smiling at the camera – breaking the fourth wall – but it’s just kind of a perfect picture. It’s unusual because he’s carrying a surfboard and Joey didn’t surf! We were just having fun at the beach. There’s a childlike aspect because he was shy. Looking like that, he knew there was no other path for him than rock’n’roll, so he’d got in a band as soon as he could.

I’d read that for shooting outside you should use Plus-X film, but this session is the only time I ever used it. Most photographers used Tri-X, because you got a better range of light and dark. Buried to the right of Joey is a Schaefer beer can, a New York beer that’s no longer made, which is a cool touch. Joey didn’t like the photo – he said, “You made my legs look thin.” Like it was my fault he had skinny legs.

Also, the Ramones never smiled. Sire used a vertical shot from my album session where they’re smiling, with the caption: “The Ramones: they’re so punky, you’re gonna love them.” They wanted them to be this cute band that would appeal to Bay City Rollers fans, but Joey went, “No way. Bury that picture. Never use it again.” After that they never smiled in photographs again, but I have this one on top of my bookshelf and it makes me very happy. I think other people like it for the same reason.

I sell more of it than the album cover photo. Eddie Vedder has a copy. Karen O has one in her kitchen. Andrew Watt, the superstar producer of Paul McCartney and the Rolling Stones, has it. I never wanted to become a professional photographer taking pictures of people I don’t know. For 98% of my career I never got paid but I had a lot of fun. I was just taking photographs of my friends.

Roberta Bayley is the recipient of the Icon award at the 2026 Abbey Road music photography awards. This year’s winners will be revealed at the awards celebration on 24 September at Abbey Road Studios, London

Entertainment.title: From petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham Parker
Entertainment.text:
To say Graham Parker enjoyed a swift rise to fame is an understatement. He played his first live show with his most famous backing band, the Rumour, in October 1975, at the Newlands Tavern, a pub in Nunhead, south-east London. By the start of the following year, he had a record deal and was in the studio recording his debut album, Howlin’ Wind. The buzz around him was such that the sessions were interrupted by the arrival of a succession of stars – Thin Lizzy’s Phil Lynott among them – intrigued to hear what the fuss was about: a petrol pump attendant from Surrey who sang like Van Morrison and had written a set of smart, sharp, literate songs in between filling up cars.

The record arrived in April 1976 to vast critical excitement, a lot of it occasioned by the album’s closing track, the reggae-influenced, attitude-laden Don’t Ask Me Questions. After Howlin’ Wind came out, followed in October by Heat Treatment, things ratcheted up another notch. Parker turned up in Australia to discover the media waiting for him and a press conference arranged in the airport: they had taken the amount of music press coverage Parker was receiving to mean he was “as big as Bruce Springsteen, which was insane”. Low down on a festival bill topped by Bob Dylan, he found himself backstage collared by the headline act, eager to tell Parker how much he loved his work. There also exists a photo of Parker in Los Angeles, with, of all people, Michael Jackson, but their meeting was apparently less successful. “I said to him: ‘Michael, great to meet you, I did a version of [Jackson 5 hit] I Want You Back recently.’ And he just sort of said: ‘Ooh.’ So that,” he laughs, “was the full extent of my conversation with Michael Jackson.”

In truth, Parker seemed an unlikely candidate for a saviour of rock. He was short and wiry, a former hippy who had taken himself off to Morocco in his teens and served time in a band called Terry Burbot’s Magic Mud: “My idea,” he sighs, “a burbot being a fish that I knew had become extinct in England because Angling Times offered £100 to anyone who could prove they’d caught one.” On returning, he went back home to Deepcut in Surrey, shorn of his “arse-length” hair, writing songs influenced not by prevalent trends (“I thought progressive rock needed to be destroyed thoroughly”), but the music he’d loved in his youth: Motown, soul, ska, “pop hits on the radio”.

On today’s video call from his home in upstate New York, ahead of a UK tour, Parker’s eyes are shielded by tinted sunglasses. Decades ago, dark glasses were his permanent look, which helped give Parker the air of a man who was almost disproportionately angry, or at least a lot angrier than his songs suggested he was. On Howlin’ Wind, he spat out the lyrics of Lady Doctor as if they were a ferocious broadside against the establishment, rather than about fancying a female GP. “Correct,” he nods. “If you went to see a band in the suburbs back then, the audience sat cross-legged, so I thought, we’ve got to do the opposite, get people up and dancing instead of sitting. So I just went out and yelled.”

The thing was, Parker didn’t seem to think his sudden rise to fame was at all unlikely. He may have looked a little incredulous in the photo of himself backstage with Dylan, but that was the exception. “Oh no, I was brimming with confidence,” he says, smiling. “I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy, you know: I’m going to be the one who shows people something that can be done – attitude, great lyrics that say something, a tight band. I got an instant record deal, I was getting all this attention and none of these people who’d been slogging around the pubs for years were. I remember one of the early gigs we did, the great Ian Dury and his minder, Fred ‘Spider’ Rowe, standing in front of the stage wearing sunglasses, trying to put the mockers on me. I thought: I’m having a great effect here. This is good! I can’t help being this good, you know!” He suddenly looks a bit concerned at revealing his youthful cockiness. “I hope,” he says quietly, “you can write this up with some humour in it. I do know I was being an idiot.”

Of course, Parker never quite became the huge star everyone seemed to think he would be in 1976. Instead, he carved out a fascinating 50-year career as a critically lauded, cult singer-songwriter whose work has ranged wildly. He recorded an album of obscure Lennon and McCartney songs with Kate Pierson of the B-52s; published novels and short stories; and maintained a pretty startling level of quality control over the course of 47 albums, despite his belief that “you should press the reset button” with every new release. His most recent, 2023’s Last Chance to Learn the Twist, was a delight, a live-sounding collection of songs that range in style from soul to prewar pop.

His career has also regularly involved Parker doing the exact opposite of what one might have expected under the circumstances. In the late 70s, dissatisfied with his then record label, Mercury, he terminated their relationship by releasing Mercury Poisoning, a spectacularly withering song that, among other accusations, suggested the label “couldn’t sell kebabs to the Greeks” (“a bit literal,” he concedes today). His commercial stock rising in the 80s US, thanks to 1979’s superb Squeezing Out Sparks album, he signed a deal with Atlantic Records, whose chair Ahmet Ertegun suggested he make his next album sound “like Phil Collins”. Parker proceeded to make the deliberately rough-hewn The Mona Lisa’s Sister: a wonderful collection of songs utterly out of step with mainstream 80s rock trends, that, one can’t help but notice, has aged rather better than most mainstream 80s rock.

In 2012, he unexpectedly found himself in Hollywood at the behest of Judd Apatow, a long-term fan: a golden opportunity that might nevertheless have given another artist pause, given that Parker was required to play himself in This Is 40, one of a plethora of underperforming artists who Paul Rudd’s record label honcho character has put his faith in. “He’s signing all these losers from the 70s and 80s. He’s got Haircut 100, and Frank Black without the Pixies, and me,” Parker says, chuckling. “When Judd told me, I said: I can do this, I could destroy his record company instantly, mate. I’m in.”

Hollywood was another entirely unexpected state of affairs. “For me, small timer, quite happy with his little career – playing grungy little solo gigs, doing records my way with no one interfering – to suddenly become this actor, pop singer thing, I didn’t see that coming. I ended up sitting in a dressing room with John Lithgow and Paul Rudd and Megan Fox, thinking, I should call a cab, I don’t belong here. But I sank into it pretty good. Being flown to Hollywood to do talks, first class, put up in these amazing hotels … I’m suddenly somebody, for five minutes. But it was a long five minutes, because the film went on and on in America, it was shown for months.”

Parker does, indeed, seem perfectly contented with his little career, grungy solo gigs and all: that’s exactly what he’s doing in the UK this month. For all his vaulting ambition in his early 20s, he is not sure that he was really cut out for fame. “The little bit of stardom I had, when everyone’s after you, everyone’s trying to grab you, that crept in and it was quite unpleasant really. Record labels start giving you too much money for music that I knew wasn’t for everybody and probably wasn’t going to burst out in platinum sales. I ended up telling my manager, tell them to pay me half what they’re offering. Which is weird, I know, but I think I did the best thing.”

Indeed, he is a vociferous advocate for keeping things small-scale. “I can pull a crowd, I can do it without the costs of a band, and it taught me to sing – I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them.” Although he has caveats. His mordantly funny 2001 song I’ll Never Play Jacksonville Again details the true story of a gig at which Parker ended up playing to “two couples, two barmen who looked like Ted Nugent, and a guy who looked a bit gormless and kept staring at one of the women’s legs until her boyfriend head-butted him. Five people in the audience and there’s a fight! How fucking often does that happen, man? I thought, this is the end.”

He says he’s been true to the song’s title and never played Jacksonville again. “But only because nobody’s offered me a gig there. If the money’s good enough and there’s two other gigs nearby, maybe I’ll do it. And I’ll do that song. It’ll be fun.”
